introduction: “The Bahá’ís should not interfere in political matters, but rather engage in educating the nation’s children, promote sciences and knowledge, strive to improve morals.” Most of these hundred quotations are ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s letters to Persia during the Constitutional Revolution of 1906–11, when each party suspected the Bahá’ís of serving the other; the last are later statements of the principle. Read in order they define it by what it permits and what it forbids. Service to the nation, obedience to government, voting, and office held with integrity are required or allowed; partisanship, sedition, and political talk in the community’s meetings are not. Religion is concerned with hearts, and its unity is lost when it is made “a tool by party politicians.” Much of this the early Christians were also told, as a small community under suspicion: render unto Caesar, honour the king, study to be quiet. Jeremiah, Confucius, Washington and Madison add their warnings against meddling and faction. But the tradition of public engagement is strong and is quoted here against the readings at many points: Pericles, Aristotle and Plato on the citizen’s duty; Mill and Roosevelt on those who look on; Thoreau on conscience; Amos and Nathan, who rebuked kings; Lincoln, who quoted “a house divided” and took a side.
questions: “Service to the nation and government is an obligation.” List what the readings require of a citizen, and what they forbid. Where is the line between them?
Pericles called the man who takes no part in public affairs “useless,” and Mill warned that bad men need only that good men do nothing. What do the readings say good people should be doing?

The early church was told to “honour the king” and “study to be quiet.” How far does the situation of a small, suspected minority explain these readings, and what in them does not depend on that situation?
Amos and Nathan spoke against kings; Thoreau went to jail rather than pay a tax. How do the readings ask a believer to respond to injustice by a government?
Washington warned of “the baneful effects of the spirit of party.” What have you seen partisanship do to a friendship, a family or a community?

Women’s suffrage is called “a political issue” in a reading that also affirms the equality on which it rests. How do principles the readings teach come to be realized in law, if not through party contest?

outside.why: Not politics but schools, science, morals and peace. Swift’s king of Brobdingnag: whoever could make two ears of corn grow where only one grew before would do more essential service to his country than the whole race of politicians put together.
Jeremiah’s letter to a religious minority in a foreign state gave the same charge: seek the peace of the city, and pray unto the Lord for it.

In a revolution, “well-wishers of all,” with “no attachment to any party nor any resentment toward any group.” Lincoln, on the eve of civil war: we are not enemies, but friends. We must not be enemies.

To serve the country “in the moral and ethical realms.” Burke on where public affection starts: to love the little platoon we belong to in society is the first link in the series by which we proceed towards a love to our country and to mankind.

“We seek to play no part in political affairs, rather do we wish the welfare of all.” Goldsmith, in lines Johnson supplied: how small, of all that human hearts endure, that part which laws or kings can cause or cure.

Non-interference does not mean refusing “to serve the nation and the government; indeed service … is an obligation.” Pericles: we regard him who takes no part in public affairs not as unambitious but as useless. Which public affairs do the readings require a believer to take part in?
A Bahá’í appointed to office must serve with integrity. Daniel under a foreign king: they could find none occasion nor fault; forasmuch as he was faithful.
Appointed, not ambitious. Plato: the State in which the rulers are most reluctant to govern is always the best and most quietly governed.

In the United States “citizens shall take part in elections”; the prohibition is against making trouble. Jesus: render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar’s; and unto God the things that are God’s.
Those without official position have no business interfering. Confucius: he who is not in any particular office has nothing to do with plans for the administration of its duties.

“Religious matters should not be confused with politics.” Jefferson: religion is a matter which lies solely between man and his God; the legislative powers of government reach actions only, and not opinions.
Jesus before the governor: my kingdom is not of this world: if my kingdom were of this world, then would my servants fight.
Political prancing builds “a mere nest”; a universal aim is “soaring in the divine atmosphere.” Paul: our conversation is in heaven.
“The path of all should be the refinement of characters.” Paul: study to be quiet, and to do your own business, and to work with your own hands.
“Strive so that complete harmony and unity may be achieved between the government and people.” Jesus: blessed are the peacemakers.

“And if you remain powerless, withdraw completely.” John Stuart Mill: bad men need nothing more to compass their ends, than that good men should look on and do nothing. When does withdrawal leave the field to the worst, and what do the readings ask believers to do instead of looking on?
Socrates explained his own withdrawal from Athenian politics: he who will really fight for the right, if he would live even for a little while, must have a private station and not a public one.
The friends want progress “but without war and strife.” James: from whence come wars and fightings among you? come they not hence, even of your lusts?
“No quarrel or contention with any faction.” Abraham to Lot: let there be no strife, I pray thee, between me and thee; for we be brethren.
“Perfect results from imperfect causes are impossible.” Thoreau: there are a thousand hacking at the branches of evil to one who is striking at the root.
“Goodwill toward all people, loyalty to the government.” Peter’s four commands: honour all men. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honour the king.
“Obedience to the government and goodwill toward all nations.” Paul to Christians in Nero’s capital: let every soul be subject unto the higher powers.
Be well-wishers to all, obey the government, do not interfere. Paul to Titus: to obey magistrates, to speak evil of no man, to be no brawlers, but gentle.
“Sincere and well-wishing toward all the governments of the world.” Washington’s advice to his country: observe good faith and justice towards all Nations; cultivate peace and harmony with all.
Diogenes, asked where he came from: I am a citizen of the world.
“Truthful, well-wishing and kind to all people.” James: the wisdom that is from above is peaceable, gentle, without partiality.
“Religion is concerned with things of the spirit, politics with things of the world.” Jesus, asked to settle an inheritance: man, who made me a judge or a divider over you?
“Our focus is the moral world.” Confucius held that this was the root of politics too: to govern means to rectify. If you lead on the people with correctness, who will dare not to be correct?

The Cause is “related to the Kingdom rather than to earthly sovereignty.” John: when Jesus perceived that they would come and take him by force, to make him a king, he departed again into a mountain himself alone.
“Human politics … is as nothing compared to divine politics.” Zechariah: not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit.
Aristotle would not have understood a human good outside the city: man is by nature a political animal. What do the readings mean by “divine politics,” and does it leave Aristotle’s claim standing?
Political affairs are “no more than a mirage” beside the Cause. The psalmist: put not your trust in princes; in that very day his thoughts perish.
“I beseech God to make you divine, not political.” Hebrews: here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come.
“Religion must never be used as a tool by party politicians.” Swift on what happens when it is: we have just enough religion to make us hate, but not enough to make us love one another.
Political power “prevents unity.” Lord Acton: power tends to corrupt, and absolute power corrupts absolutely.
“The Cause of God is sanctified from all political power.” Jesus: the princes of the Gentiles exercise dominion over them. But it shall not be so among you.
A hope that “the existing competition between the powers may pass away.” Micah: nation shall not lift up a sword against nation; they shall sit every man under his vine and under his fig tree.

Women’s suffrage “is a political issue and I am detached from all political matters”; yet women and men are two wings. Susan B. Anthony made the same principle a political claim and was arrested for voting: it was we, the people; not we, the male citizens; but we, the whole people, who formed the Union. How does a principle advance when its teachers stay out of the contest?
With a political man, speak “with wisdom and moderation,” and only of oneness. Ecclesiastes: the words of wise men are heard in quiet more than the cry of him that ruleth among fools.
“We came to meet the poor, not to see kings and princes.” Jesus: when thou makest a feast, call the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind.
A reputation for honesty made the statement believed. Paul’s defence: neither against the law, neither against the temple, nor yet against Caesar, have I offended any thing at all.
A prisoner for religion was suspected of planning to “raise the banner of independence.” The charge against Paul: a pestilent fellow, and a mover of sedition.
And the charge that decided Pilate: whosoever maketh himself a king speaketh against Caesar.
A community with “no intention or purpose except the peace and wellbeing of humanity.” Isaiah: the work of righteousness shall be peace.
No part in “political movements which lead to sedition.” Proverbs: meddle not with them that are given to change.

Thoreau refused a tax and went to jail: must the citizen ever for a moment resign his conscience to the legislator? We should be men first, and subjects afterward. Where do the readings place conscience when a government does wrong?

Wordsworth remembered what a revolution felt like at its beginning: bliss was it in that dawn to be alive. The Persian revolution ended, the reading says, “in lawlessness and rebellion.” What did those who stood aside give up, and what were they spared?
“Be occupied with your own professions and your own affairs.” Plato’s definition of justice: doing one’s own business, and not being a busybody.
Occupy yourselves with your own work “with perfect sanctity and detachment.” Ecclesiastes: better is an handful with quietness, than both the hands full with travail and vexation of spirit.
“Concentrate all their thoughts on teaching.” Paul: no man that warreth entangleth himself with the affairs of this life.
“We … make no mention of anything except the chanting of clear verses.” Jesus: seek ye first the kingdom of God.
“We do not speak about political matters.” Proverbs: it is an honour for a man to cease from strife: but every fool will be meddling.
“Do not interfere in political matters.” Proverbs: he that meddleth with strife belonging not to him is like one that taketh a dog by the ears.
“Don’t talk about politics. Speak about the good work” that has been done. Paul: whatsoever things are of good report, think on these things.
“The party of God is forbidden from interfering in political matters.” Washington to his country: let me warn you in the most solemn manner against the baneful effects of the spirit of party.

The friends “must not discuss politics even in private.” Socrates held a private station and still would not be silent: I am that gadfly which God has given the state, all day long arousing and persuading and reproaching you. What kind of speech about public life do the readings leave open?
The psalmist’s restraint: neither do I exercise myself in great matters, or in things too high for me.

In a revolution each side accused the Bahá’ís of serving the other. Madison on how parties see: so strong is this propensity of mankind to fall into mutual animosities, that the most frivolous distinctions have been sufficient to kindle their unfriendly passions.

“Remain aloof and wish well to both sides.” The Qur’án asks more of a peacemaker: if two parties of believers fall to fighting, make peace between them; and if one party doeth wrong to the other, fight ye that which doeth wrong. Is there a wrong so plain that neutrality between the parties fails?
“Obedience to the government and well-wishing toward the nation.” Paul: render therefore to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due; honour to whom honour.

They “strived for reform and unity, and when unable to achieve this, withdrew.” Proverbs: the beginning of strife is as when one letteth out water: therefore leave off contention, before it be meddled with.

Neither affinity with the government in power nor enmity toward other parties. Jefferson after a bitter election: every difference of opinion is not a difference of principle. We are all Republicans, we are all Federalists.
The Bahá’ís “did not side with anyone.” Paul: if ye bite and devour one another, take heed that ye be not consumed one of another.
“Each of the parties took up a pickaxe and struck at the foundation of Iran.” Jesus: if a kingdom be divided against itself, that kingdom cannot stand.

Lincoln quoted that verse and then took a side: I believe this government cannot endure, permanently half slave and half free. When a house is divided over a question of right, what do the readings ask of those who refuse a party?

Critics asked why ‘Abdu’l-Bahá did not help the nationalists against despotism. Plato: he who refuses to rule is liable to be ruled by one who is worse than himself. What reasons does the reading give, and do they answer Plato?
“Let these events pass. Thereafter the wisdom thereof shall become plain.” Jesus to Peter: what I do thou knowest not now; but thou shalt know hereafter.

Do not “harmonize with political parties.” Washington on the spirit of party: it agitates the Community with ill-founded jealousies and false alarms; kindles the animosity of one part against another.
“Withdraw from all … Leave them to their vain pursuits.” The Qur’án on factions: no concern at all hast thou with them. Their case will go to Allah.
“Stand aside and be detached.” An early Christian’s description of his community: as citizens, they share in all things with others, and yet endure all things as if foreigners.
Take refuge “in reliance upon the Ancient Truth.” Isaiah to a kingdom tempted by alliances: in quietness and in confidence shall be your strength.

“Complete calm and composure, not interfering.” The prophets of Israel did not keep to it: Amos hath conspired against thee; the land is not able to bear all his words. Was Amos interfering in politics? What is the difference between his speech and a party’s?
Nathan before King David: thou art the man. What, in these readings, takes the place of the prophet’s rebuke of a ruler?
They “fulfilled their duties and never entered into corruption.” John the Baptist to tax collectors and soldiers: exact no more than that which is appointed you; do violence to no man.
Bahá’u’lláh “explicitly forbade the loved ones from involvement in political affairs and commanded” obedience. Peter: submit yourselves to every ordinance of man for the Lord’s sake.
The Qur’án: obey Allah, and obey the messenger and those of you who are in authority.
Aloofness becomes “a source of confidence for all governments.” Paul asks prayers for kings, and for all that are in authority; that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life.
Those who meddled “alone suffered the consequences.” Jesus to the disciple who drew a sword for him: all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword.
Repeated elections and assemblies in Persia “have borne no fruit.” Pope: for forms of government let fools contest; whate’er is best administer’d is best.
The friends became “dear even to their enemies.” Proverbs: when a man’s ways please the Lord, he maketh even his enemies to be at peace with him.

“We have nothing to do with political tricks and chicaneries.” Machiavelli taught them as the craft itself: a wise lord cannot, nor ought he to, keep faith when such observance may be turned against him. Can public affairs be conducted without what he describes? What would the readings put in its place?
Those “absorbed by personal interests or political affairs degraded … themselves.” Even among the twelve: there was a strife among them, which of them should be accounted the greatest.
To abstain from “party politics.” Paul found parties inside the church: every one of you saith, I am of Paul; and I of Apollos. Is Christ divided?
Political matters are never to be raised in the consultative assembly. Paul: that there be no divisions among you; but that ye be perfectly joined together in the same mind.
If anyone wishes to “criticize those in authority, others should not agree.” Exodus: thou shalt not curse the ruler of thy people.
The Assembly must not “breathe a word about political affairs.” The Qur’án: dispute not one with another lest ye falter and your strength depart from you.
A meeting was dissolved because it was whispered to be political. The whisper is old: we found this fellow perverting the nation, and forbidding to give tribute to Caesar.
A convention founded on “love and kindness and the promotion of the oneness of the human world.” The Qur’án: hold fast, all of you together, to the cable of Allah, and do not separate.

A newspaper must not “write a single word against the government.” Milton pleaded for an unlicensed press: let Truth and Falshood grapple; who ever knew Truth put to the wors, in a free and open encounter? What is the difference between his claim for a nation and this counsel to a small, suspected community?
Asked about constitutional government: “our concern is with the heart and the soul.” Confucius on what a state cannot do without: the confidence of the people in their ruler.

“We have no attachment to these issues.” Theodore Roosevelt had little patience with those outside: the credit belongs to the man who is actually in the arena. In what arena do the readings place the believer?
“Thy task concerneth the life of the soul.” Jesus to Martha: thou art careful and troubled about many things: but one thing is needful.
“Except to speak well of them, make thou no mention of the earth’s kings.” Peter: let none of you suffer as a busybody in other men’s matters.

Asked about joining the Socialist party: the Bahá’í Cause “comprehends all the degrees.” The Communist Manifesto offered its own all-comprehending unity: working men of all countries, unite! What is the difference between a unity of all and a unity of one class against another?

To work “for one political party to overcome another” negates the spirit of the Faith. Madison’s definition: a number of citizens united by some common impulse of passion, or of interest, adverse to the rights of other citizens.
The Qur’án on the same habit in religion: each sect exulting in its tenets.

“Nonacceptance of political posts.” Burke thought a seat in parliament a trust worth holding: your representative owes you, not his industry only, but his judgment. What does a society lose when people of conscience decline office, and what does this community judge it would lose by accepting?

“We cannot start judging how a particular government came into power.” Thoreau: any man more right than his neighbors constitutes a majority of one already. Which of them trusts the individual’s judgment of governments, and why does the reading not?
Believers will subordinate even their own laws to the requirements of their governments. Jesus held that he owed no temple tax, and paid it: notwithstanding, lest we should offend them.
Bahá’í institutions do not set themselves against those of the country. Proverbs: hatred stirreth up strifes: but love covereth all sins.
